Photograph: Reuters Ukraine Ukraine drone strike on oil refinery deep inside Russia kills at least 13 Attack hundreds of miles from border would be among deadliest of war as Kyiv aims to strangle Russian economy Luke Harding and agencies Mon 10 Aug 2026 12.25 EDT First published on Mon 10 Aug 2026 11.12 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A Ukrainian drone strike on an industrial city deep inside Russia has killed at least 13 people, according to the local mayor, as Kyiv steps up its campaign of long-range strikes on targets far from the frontline. Kyiv said it hit the Taneco refinery in the city of Nizhnekamsk, about 750 miles (1,200km) from the Ukrainian border. Footage circulating online appeared to show smoke rising from the refinery. Ukraine’s general staff said the raid was part of a campaign to reduce the “military potential of the Russian aggressor”. Russian investigators claimed civilian and industrial sites in the city had been hit. The head of the Tatarstan region, Rustam Minnikhanov, said a Ukrainian drone hit a hostel, killing nine people. He posted images showing a badly damaged building. If the death toll is confirmed, the strike would be among the deadliest Ukrainian attacks on Russian territory since the full-scale invasion began in 2022, underscoring the growing reach of Kyiv’s strikes deep inside Russia. Map showing location of Nizhnekamsk in Russia The Uzbek consulate said in a Telegram post that seven of the victims were Uzbek citizens. Minnikhanov declared a day of mourning and Russian prosecutors opened a criminal case into alleged terrorism. Local video footage showed Ukrainian drones buzzing above the city’s skyline, flying low over grey and box-like Soviet-era apartment blocks. Two plumes of black smoke could be seen rising above an industrial zone on the wooded outskirts of Nizhnekamsk. View image in fullscreen Ukraine’s armed forces hit equipment depots and a repair unit in the occupied Donetsk on Sunday night. Photograph: Anadolu/Getty Images The site is home to Taneco, one of Russia’s biggest and most technologically advanced oil refineries, owned by Tatneft. It also houses a plant that produces rubber and petrochemical products. Ukraine also bombed the area in June. In an address on Sunday, Volodymyr Zelenskyy said “long-range sanctions” against the Kremlin and its war machine would continue. In recent months Ukrainian drones have wreaked havoc on Russia’s oil export industry, even hitting refineries in Siberia, 1,500 miles from the frontline. The governor of the Tyumen region in western Siberia said on Monday that several Ukrainian drones had fallen on an industrial facility and that emergency services were dealing with a fire. There have been several strikes on warehouses belonging to Wildberries, Russia’s equivalent of Amazon, as well as on oil tankers in the Sea of Azov and Black Sea. Ukraine’s long-term goal is to slowly strangle the Russian economy so Moscow can no longer fund its war. 3:41 Who has the momentum in the Russia-Ukraine war? – video explainer Zelenskyy described his country’s remote bombing campaign as “entirely justified”. “Every Russian strike [on Ukrainian towns and cities] will be met with our response. Russia’s war will be felt more and more at their own home – in Russia,” he said on social media. “The only reason this is still continuing is Russia’s unwillingness to end this war.” Russia’s defence ministry said it had intercepted 456 Ukrainian drones flying above Russian territory and annexed Crimea. Ukraine says it is knocking out its opponent’s air defence systems more quickly than they can be replaced, creating air corridors or “doors” it can exploit. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every day Sign up to Headlines Europe A digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week day Preview latest after newsletter promotion View image in fullscreen Four people, including a child, were injured in Russian strikes on Zaporizhzhia. Photograph: Anadolu/Getty Images Overnight, Ukraine’s armed forces hit equipment depots and a repair unit in the occupied Donetsk and Luhansk parts of eastern Ukraine, while ⁠Russian-appointed local authorities said the ⁠Zaporizhzhia region in south-east Ukraine was largely without ⁠electricity on Monday ⁠after ​Ukrainian attacks destroyed key power facilities. On Russia’s Black Sea ⁠coast, power outages were ​reported in ‌parts of ‌Novorossiysk, a major export ‌port, and in the holiday resort of Gelendzhik, regional authorities said on Telegram. Blinded by War: documenting the aftermath of injury in Ukraine – photo essay Read more There were unconfirmed reports that Russian ballistic missile launcher systems were destroyed inside Russia, not far from the border. According to Telegram channels citing Ukrainian military sources, the targeted high-value military assets were in Russia’s western Kursk and Bryansk regions. Both were used to launch Iskander and hypersonic Zircon missiles towards Kyiv. Ukrainian prosecutors said five people were killed on Sunday in a Russian artillery strike on a village outside Kharkiv. Several houses were flattened as a result of an “enemy strike” on Buhaivka in the Chuhuiv district, they said. Sweden’s security service, Säpo, said on Monday it ⁠had shut down a Russian spying operation that had tried to ⁠influence decision making ⁠there ​and discredit the Nordic country as well as its EU and ⁠Nato allies. Säpo said the operation had been planned and directed by Russia’s SVR foreign ⁠intelligence service and involved three people working under ​the cover of ‌diplomatic immunity. “This is ‌consistent with the threat we see Russia posing,” a Säpo spokesperson said. “We have been able to monitor ​what happened at these meetings between the individuals involved, what was said and what assignments were given. They are ⁠no longer in Sweden and we ​have ​been able to break up ​this operation.” Explore more on these topics Ukraine Russia Drones (military) Europe news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story Blinded by War: documenting the aftermath of injury in Ukraine – photo essay Zelenskyy calls for more air defences as Russian attack on Kyiv kills at least 17 Ukrainian drone attacks on Black Sea resort and Crimea kill 11, Russia claims Russian missile destroys US firm’s Kyiv drone factory ‘Lenin was an enemy of humanity’: Why Kyiv wants to put Cossack chief statue in place of Soviet leader Rising Zelenskyy and falling Netanyahu cross paths in chaotic White House Burnham’s Ukraine gambit is a symbolic start for PM who wants to look inward Romania summons Russia’s ambassador after downing third drone since Friday Ukraine strikes on Russia’s ‘Amazon’ warehouses bring war closer to ordinary people Mykhailo Drapatyi: Ukrainians hope new commander will end army’s ‘Soviet culture’ Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

https://euobserver.com/237930/we-lied-to.text: Every day, the Ukraine Battlefield update newsletter offers a clear look at how the war is unfolding on the ground. Subscribe for free here to get the full text delivered to your inbox. The Russian front near Lyman is retreating, bringing significant relief to Sloviansk. Ukraine was initially meant to fall within three days; now Putin adviser Patrushev is making the same threat to Poland. 77 percent of Ukrainians want to continue resisting through the winter even without electricity and heating, with Kyiv residents the most determined. Another Russian general has been killed — his unit is fighting near Kostiantynivka. Map of the day — Lyman according to the Russians. Videos of the day — an election campaign advert on Russian television; Ukrainian depots burn just like Russian ones; a Ukrainian grandmother takes apart a Russian drone; an interceptor drone armed with a shotgun shoots down an enemy craft over a frontline city. The Russian front near Lyman is retreating, bringing significant relief to Sloviansk. The situation near Orikhiv is gradually deteriorating, while Russians are continuing to push near Dobropillia, Kostiantynivka, Sloviansk and Kramatorsk, as well as in the north of Kharkiv region. Russian Z-channels are reporting on each of these locations in a way that leaves no room for doubt about the Russian army’s successes. But alongside celebratory and objectively nonsensical claims — most recently, for example, several Russian sources claimed that Orikhiv had been captured — Russians are also debating their defeat near Lyman. The same accounts that eagerly exaggerate and publish false information are once again complaining that things went badly near Lyman because someone in the army lied to both them and Russian president Vladimir Putin. This comes two weeks after Putin, relying on military reports, announced the capture of the town of Sviatohirsk. Today, Russians report that the front is already 27 km further east and that Ukrainian soldiers are advancing even further across the Zherebets river. “Alongside strikes on the Ukrainian rear and the Russian army’s successes near Orikhiv and Dobropillia, the consequences of excessively embellished reports continue to emerge in the Lyman direction,” the major Telegram channel Rybar wrote. Just two weeks ago, Rybar itself was drawing entirely nonsensical maps. It is now publishing relatively detailed information that completely changes the picture of the battle for the northern flank of the Sloviansk-Kramatorsk urban area. “The enemy’s 3rd Army Corps and units subordinate to it have moved into active operations and achieved tactical successes that call into question a further assault on the city itself,” Rybar wrote about Russia’s prospects of capturing Lyman, the gateway to Sloviansk from the north-east. Rybar’s map now looks entirely different. There is no longer any trace of the salient north of Lyman, and it is covered with blue arrows showing the directions of Ukrainian attacks. Ukrainian units are in Novoselivka, Yarova, Oleksandrivka and Seredne, Rybar acknowledged, but it merely repeated the names of villages confirmed in a video by Ukraine’s 3rd Army Corps on Tuesday (15 September). According to independent analysts, some footage in the compilation is several months old and the situation is considerably more favourable to Ukraine than the Russians themselves admit. As we have already written, this is the result of an operation named Vivaldi because it has four phases, and this is the first. “To be continued!” were the words concluding the 3rd Corps’ post. Українські прапори над очищеною від окупантів землею! Бійці Третього армійського корпусу та приданих підрозділів повернули синьо-жовті стяги у населених пунктах Середнє, Новоселівка, Ярова та на околицях Корового Яру. Операція «Вівальді». Сезон перший. Далі буде! pic.twitter.com/o6k55y7UkD — Третій армійський корпус (@ab3army) September 15, 2026 The next step may be an attempt to cross the Zherebets river. Rybar claimed that this was already happening: “According to some reports, Ukrainian sabotage groups that crossed the Zherebets river in the area of the Zhuravka ravine are operating east of the river and are attempting to enter the villages of Terny and Yampolivka. Supplies for the Russian bridgehead west of Lyman passed through them, and enemy activity at this location points to a difficult situation on both banks of the river.” Rybar claimed that this was not a strategic defeat, but that the setback would delay the assault on Sloviansk. This was partly because units attacking it from the east no longer have their flank protected against counter-attacks from the north. Another Russian, Oleg Tsarev, wondered why the entire operation was being conducted in complete silence on the Ukrainian side, given that, in his view, Kyiv needed to highlight a success in order to show its allies that it could continue fighting. “It must be said that this is an effective tactic. If they were loudly announcing [their successes], the leadership of the Russian Federation would hear them. But now, it seems, the information is not reaching the top. War correspondents, with rare exceptions, are silent: nobody wants trouble. Ukraine is silent too,” Tsarev invoked the old Russian trope of a good ruler whose incompetent boyars lie to him and thereby ruin his plans. He omitted the fact that people like him are part of the problem. So did Yuri Kotenok, who otherwise draws entirely fabricated maps. It was he who now announced the capture of Orikhiv and speculated about the suspicious Ukrainian silence. He even warned against a repeat of the story of the allegedly captured Kupiansk and other similar places — although he himself had loudly celebrated it. The final sentence of Kotenok’s post is true in that the 3rd Army Corps is indeed a very high-quality formation and includes elite units. The rest, however, mainly serves as an example of the Russian way of reporting on the war: “The enemy attacking near Lyman with mechanised groups is battle-hardened and experienced. They are not frightened conscripts — drug addicts or disoriented scum — but fully motivated Nazis from Azov… Has there not been enough playing around with murderers? And yes, open your eyes, those of you who still keep them shut; open your ears, those of you with plugs in them: fighting and retreating is not shameful; what is shameful is concealing things and lying, including to the Supreme Commander.” Paradoxically, the DeepStateUA map of this area fully corresponds with what the Russians are writing — the Ukrainians are completely silent. Ukraine was initially meant to fall within three days; now Putin adviser Patrushev is making the same threat to Poland. “If Russia attacked us and if we did not throw in the towel, I think we would defeat Russia quite quickly. We have overwhelming air superiority over Russia… If Ukrainians were able to take out half of Russia’s refining capacity in six months, we would be able to take out the other half in six weeks,” Polish foreign minister Radek Sikorski said at a conference in Kyiv. He did not mean Poland alone, but Nato as a whole, including in the event that the United States betrayed its allies and did not help them. At this point, it is not important whether this is a realistic scenario. At a time of escalating Russian provocations, Poland — and Sikorski personally — are communicating with the Kremlin in a way intended to make clear that they are not afraid of it and will not yield to Putin. The Polish minister’s statement quite naturally provoked a strong reaction. After returning home, he published a short post repeating the same point: “… thanks to air superiority, the air forces of Nato’s European component, even without US involvement, would be able to destroy half of Russia’s refineries faster than Ukraine. I still think so.” Żeby było jasne co powiedziałem w Kijowie. Że w wypadku rosyjskiej agresji na NATO, dzięki przewadze w powietrzu, lotnictwo europejskiej części NATO byłoby w stanie, nawet bez udziału USA, zniszczyć połowę rosyjskich rafinerii szybciej niż Ukraina. Nadal tak uważam. — Radosław Sikorski 🇵🇱🇪🇺 (@sikorskiradek) September 14, 2026 As Sikorski is Polish, his remarks quite naturally received the most attention in Poland. This included criticism, of course. But military analyst Jaroslaw Wolski strongly praised the minister. He believes that this is precisely the language in which Russia should be addressed: “Sikorski told the truth — hence the outcry from Russia’s fifth column after his remarks. And the laughter of fools who do not understand that perhaps Poland alone would not, but Poland, Finland, Denmark, Norway and Sweden together have greater air power than Russia. Adding France, Germany, the United Kingdom or Italy makes the balance hopeless for Russia. And this must be made clear.” According to Wolski, Russia is an “air dwarf”. He referred to a consensus among analysts that Nato’s European component alone would gain complete air superiority within a month and would be able to strike targets deep inside Russian territory. “Threatening people with Gerans, Kh-101s and Iskanders makes sense only if you can produce them in large numbers, and Russia would very soon be unable to do that. The factories would be destroyed, forcing production to be dispersed and reducing its volume,” the Polish analyst added. Determining the real strength of air forces is not so straightforward. Official statistics state that Russia’s military air force has a total of 4,237 aircraft, while Nato armies have 20,375. But this includes everything from the most modern combat aircraft to non-combat support types. Comparing combat aircraft alone, Nato has an approximately 4.5-fold advantage with the US included, and not quite a twofold advantage without the United States. It is still sufficient, exactly as Sikorski and Wolski argue. Moreover, there is a significant difference between official statistics and the real situation. The Russian air force is suffering losses and its aircraft are being technically worn down by intensive combat deployment, meaning that the number of genuinely combat-ready aircraft is considerably lower than statistical yearbooks suggest. This also applies to Western air forces, though to a lesser degree. For a simple reason: their aircraft are not fighting. Another point in Nato’s favour, including its European component, is its technological superiority. Finland, Denmark, the Netherlands, Belgium, Norway and now Poland are either extensively re-equipping, or have already re-equipped, with fifth-generation F-35 aircraft. Russia lags significantly behind in both numbers and quality. It classifies the Su-37 as a fifth-generation aircraft, but it does not, for example, achieve the same level of stealth as the F-35. Back to Sikorski. The crucial part of his statement comes at the very beginning, which starts with the words: “If Russia attacked us…”. The Polish foreign minister therefore clearly framed his claim as self-defence against a Russian attack. Under no circumstances did he even suggest that Nato would launch an unprovoked attack on Russia. That did not prevent Russia from offering an entirely different narrative at home. This week, Putin adviser Nikolai Patrushev, who is speculated to be a possible successor to Putin, implicitly but unmistakably threatened Poland with nuclear weapons : “If Poland uses military force against Russia, our country will use its entire arsenal of forces and resources, and Polish statehood will cease to exist within two or three days.” To underline what exactly he meant by the entire arsenal, Patrushev added that Sikorski assessed Russia’s military strength amateurishly and “refuses to understand that, during the special military operation, the Russian armed forces are by no means using their full potential”. Russia has thus returned to rhetoric that failed it in Ukraine and remains the subject of ridicule to this day. To illustrate the extent to which this is a militarised society fixated on war, it is worth looking at the official pre-election advert for Duma elections. It is broadcast on state television, was created using AI and, instead of a political programme, essentially tells Russians through historical figures from the Middle Ages to the second world war only that they are in a war that will continue, and that they should be prepared to die for the state. Russian state TV is using AI slop featuring historical warring figures such as Alexander Nevsky, Kutuzov and Zhukov as well as those currently fighting in Ukraine to promote this weekend’s parliamentary election pic.twitter.com/Hs8HaItN2D — Francis Scarr (@francis_scarr) September 15, 2026 77 percent of Ukrainians want to continue resisting. This follows from a new survey by the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology, a respected Ukrainian public-opinion polling agency. The pollsters asked respondents whether Ukraine should continue resisting even if Russia attacks energy infrastructure during the winter, resulting in electricity, heating and sewage outages. 77 percent of respondents supported continuing the fight, 12 percent supported accepting Russia’s terms, and 11 percent were undecided. Surprisingly, Kyiv residents — who suffered most during the previous winter and are certain to face the same now — gave the highest share of positive responses, at 83 percent. Respondents from eastern Ukraine showed the least willingness to continue resisting, but even there more than two-thirds supported it: 68 percent. Even more interesting are the responses broken down by whether respondents trust president Volodymyr Zelensky. Of those who do, as many as 89 percent support continuing the fight. But 65 percent of those who do not trust Zelensky also responded positively. This group clearly had the highest share of those who would surrender to Russia: 20 percent. Another Russian general has been killed — his unit is fighting near Kostiantynivka. Russian sources first reported this shortly before midnight on Tuesday. Among them was the Z-channel run by Yuri Kotenok, which published a photograph of the dead man and basic information about him. The officer was Major General Anton Grunis, who commanded the 4th Guards Motor Rifle Brigade. As recently as 28 August, Putin awarded him the Gold Star of Hero of Russia for the “liberation” of Kostiantynivka. The minor problem is that Ukrainian soldiers are still present in Kostiantynivka. The so-called Suvorov Brotherhood, a group of graduates of the Suvorov officer school in Kazan, was the first to confirm the report. Grunis fought in Chechnya, Georgia and Syria — that is, everywhere Russia pursued its imperial policy. He entered the reserves in 2021 but returned to the army after the invasion began. Grunis took command of the 4th Brigade in May 2023, when it was fighting for Klishchiivka near Bakhmut. He replaced its previous commander, who had been killed together with his staff in a Ukrainian army missile strike. The brigade later fought for Chasiv Yar and is currently deployed near Kostiantynivka. On Wednesday morning, Magyar’s Birds — the nickname of an elite Ukrainian army drone unit — also confirmed the report that the general had been killed. According to its post, Grunis was the seventh commander at brigade, division or army level killed by Magyar’s Birds. Their commander, Robert Brovdi, announced that Grunis “was eliminated on 12 September 2026 in his night shelter in temporarily occupied territory of Donetsk region”. Magyar update on General Grunis: “A man with a Lithuanian surname, born in Kazan, is fighting brilliantly” – putin on General Grunis (“Grozny”), who reported in July on the complete capture of Kostiantynivka and subsequently received the Hero of russia title. As a man with a… pic.twitter.com/R95bgOACAO — 414 Magyar's Birds (@414magyarbirds) September 16, 2026 Videos of the day A Ukrainian drone shot down a Russian one using a shotgu

(Zsolt Szigetvary /MTI via AP) (Zsolt Szigetvary/Zsolt Szigetvary/MTI via AP) By JUSTIN SPIKE, Associated Press September 29, 2026 at 10:30 am EDT BUDAPEST, Hungary — Hungary will soon release tens of thousands of records previously restricted to broad public access that identify people listed by the Communist-era state security services as officers, informants, collaborators or recruitment targets during Hungary's 20th-century dictatorship. The country, which peacefully transitioned to democracy in 1990 as the Soviet Union crumbled, spent more than four decades under Communist rule during which a sprawling state security apparatus closely monitored citizens and their loyalty to the socialist government. The security service, in addition to its established agents and officers, recruited private citizens, often through blackmail or under other types of duress, to monitor their coworkers, friends, neighbors and relatives, and to report on them to their handlers. The upcoming release of the files, which the Historical Archives of the State Security Services said on Tuesday will occur in two phases beginning on Nov. 4, is part of a push by Hungary's new center-right government to introduce more transparency in the workings of the state. Following a news conference at the archive on Tuesday, Gergő Bendegúz Cseh, the archive's director-general, told The Associated Press that the question of whether to release the files has been contentious since Hungary's democratic transition 36 years ago — largely, he said, because their release would likely have implicated acting politicians. “This is an old debate. Hungarian society has not been able to swallow or spit out this problem since the change of regime,” Cseh said. But shortly after his Tisza party defeated former Hungarian leader Viktor Orbán in a landslide election in April, Prime Minister Péter Magyar , 45, said that his new government would "fulfill one of the most important promises of the democratic transition: we will make the existing records public and searchable." Previously only available to close relatives of those named in the records and to researchers, the files — which the archive estimates contain around 50,000-60,000 names — will be available through a searchable, online database. Users will be able to request information on security officers, informants or recruitment targets based on their name, date or place of birth, mother’s name, code name and document type or number. Some documents will be redacted to protect sensitive personal information, including health records, addictions, sexual activity and sexual orientation. Expecting heavy traffic on the site, the archive has outsourced the database to external servers to avoid overloading its own. A second wave of releases is scheduled to occur on Feb. 25, when about 9,000 “B dossiers” — files running up to hundreds of pages each detailing individual recruits or recruitment targets — will be made public. Cseh, the archive’s director, said that successor governments to dictatorships rarely disclose the names of previous agents and informants, let alone records as detailed as those Hungary is preparing to release. “Such radical disclosures have never happened anywhere before,” Cseh said. “Now we can really understand who were the secret collaborators or informants of the state security.” Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text: Beijing has doubled down on robotics – also known as embodied AI – as the key to rolling out the technology across society. Photograph: China News Service/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Beijing has doubled down on robotics – also known as embodied AI – as the key to rolling out the technology across society. Photograph: China News Service/Getty Images China Chinese markets lose trillions as race for AI supremacy with US takes its toll Lack of profits and the threat posed by western countries are raising concern about the sustainability of Beijing’s AI boom Amy Hawkins in Beijing Tue 27 Oct 2026 00.42 EDT Last modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 01.09 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Trillions of dollars have been wiped from China’s stock markets in recent months amid increasing anxiety about the future of artificial intelligence, as Beijing races against the United States for dominance in the sector. The STAR 50 Index, which tracks technology and innovation companies on the Shanghai stock exchange, has plunged 40% since June. Other indexes of major companies dropped by about 20% over the same time period. The precipitous drop has wiped out $2.4tn from the Chinese stock market since May, according to Bloomberg. AI stocks account for over 40% of the stock market value in China and Hong Kong, according to Goldman Sachs, meaning that any dent in value will send shockwaves across the whole domestic market. US bans use of China’s DeepSeek AI tools by government agencies Read more The fall suggests that despite the government’s best efforts to boost China’s technology industries, particularly those which harness the power of AI, the domestic economy does not have the power to sustain a booming market. The Chinese government has invested heavily into AI, including a 60bn yuan state-backed AI investment fund which started pumping money into domestic developers this month. But Chinese consumers have proved stubbornly reluctant to part with their cash in many parts of the economy – including technology – meaning that many tech companies struggle to turn a profit. The lack of profits is one of several reasons for the sell-off. Another is the threat of western countries, especially the US, extending bans on Chinese technology. “This year, the profit margin is not as good as expected. And the US is raising rates. And China’s domestic demand is so weak,” said Dan Wang, the China director for the Eurasia Group. She said that there was a “general anxiety” among technology companies about whether or not the state-backed model would work in the face of weak consumer demand. The US has banned humanoid robots from China , citing national security risks, and is thought to be considering a ban on Chinese components in data centres. China is heavily reliant on exports and restrictions in the US hurt its domestic companies, which struggle to sell enough products at home. As China races with the US to pull ahead in AI, Beijing has doubled down on robotics – also known as embodied AI – as the key to rolling out the technology across society. Robotics is also seen as the answer to China’s demographic problems, such as the ageing population and the shrinking workforce. But the demand for robotics is being driven by government agencies and research institutions, rather than everyday consumers, for whom the products are still too expensive and not yet practical for home use. Humanoid robotics and robotic dogs have been popular in the entertainment industry but are yet to be useful in home settings. Shares in Unitree, China’s leading robot-maker, have halved since they started trading in August. “It doesn’t look like embodied intelligence could turn into profits in the in the mass market,” said Wang. Thin profit margins, rising rates in the US, and weak domestic demand were all contributing to a “general anxiety” among technology companies, she said. View image in fullscreen Humanoid robotics and robotic dogs have been popular in the entertainment industry but are yet to be useful in home settings. Photograph: Costfoto/NurPhoto/Shutterstock China’s government wants local investors to invest their money domestically. China has in recent months restricted overseas investment, with more regulations taking effect from 1 December, but these moves have not led to greater investment in the Chinese markets. Wang added that there was still optimism in other technology sectors, such as AI research and satellites, the latter because their links to the military indicates long term state support for the sector. And globally the AI boom is expected to last for at least another year. On Monday, US AI company Anthropic, which makes the chatbot Claude, filed paperwork ahead of a planned IPO that could be the biggest stock market debuts of all time. The company is expected to bring in as much as $100bn. China has no such blockbuster IPOs on the horizon. And despite pressure on policymakers to introduce stimulus measures to boost investment, none are expected to be announced during a politically sensitive period in China. This week the top officials in the Chinese Communist party are gathering for the fifth plenum , an important meeting that will lay the groundwork for next year’s 21st Party Congress. The Congress is expected to anoint Xi Jinping, China’s leader, for a fourth term. There is no appetite for risky or potentially destabilising policy measures before then, even if there is a chance they could boost the economy. Any stimulus measure would be “high risk”, Wang said. “What if it doesn’t work out? Then whoever came up with that policy, that guy would be held accountable”. https://www.politico.eu/article/french-g.text: PARIS — The French government explored ways of blocking social networks during last Saturday's protests, two people familiar with the plan told POLITICO. In the week leading up to Oct. 24, the French interior ministry was in touch with telecom operators to explore ways of cutting access to social networks or even to mobile internet in specific areas to prevent rioters from coordinating, according to one government official from the Prime Minister's office and one employee of a telecom company. The push culminated in Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu directly asking French telecom operators to be ready to block access to TikTok, Instagram, Snapchat and X, in a letter revealed by French digital outlet Blast, which first reported on the government's request. Advertisement Advertisement Contacted by POLITICO, officials from Lecornu's office, the technology ministry and the interior ministry did not deny the move nor the letter's existence. The government feared that the scenes of violence seen on Oct. 17 could repeat or escalate on the following weekend — a concern that did not materialize, as far fewer incidents were recorded on Oct. 24. “What they wanted, above all, was to block the communication channels that allow gangs to meet up and organize,” said the employee of a telecommunications provider, who was granted anonymity to speak freely. The move, however, would have also prevented peaceful protesters from communicating as well. Blocking access to social networks in a targeted area, such as a specific neighborhood, is not technically possible, while cutting access to mobile internet would cause major disruptions to other key services such as mobile payments, security-surveillance devices and emergency communications. The government also considered a less radical solution that would disable geolocation display features “to prevent gatherings of people who don’t know each other, for example,” according to the official from the prime minister’s office. Other limitations on social media access are being discussed in parliament as part of the debate on the so-called “who breaks pays” bill, which would hold people who "knowingly took part" in a riot financially responsible — whether or not they committed property damage themselves. The same bill would require platforms to remove within 24 hours content that incites physical or sexual assault, theft, destruction, or property damage, “when such content is likely to cause a serious disturbance to public order” and within one hour content that encourages insurrection. Other lawmakers are proposing measures ranging from tracking troublemakers via algorithmic video surveillance to penalizing online marketplaces that fail to prevent the sale of stolen goods.
